civs.name: Aegeans (Minoans & Mycenaeans)
civs.region: Crete, the Aegean islands and mainland Greece
civs.blurb: Minoan Crete and Mycenaean Greece built palace economies and sea trade across the Aegean. Their collapse around 1200 BCE left the Greek-speaking world that later produced classical Greece.

civs.name: Egyptians
civs.blurb: Farming the Nile's yearly flood let Egypt build one of the first states, with writing, pyramids and a 365-day calendar. Its wealth and know-how shaped its neighbors for 3,000 years.

civs.name: Hittites
civs.blurb: Hittite kings in Anatolia fielded chariot armies and made one of the earliest known peace treaties, with Egypt (c. 1259 BCE). Their fall around 1180 BCE opened Syria to new states.

civs.name: Amorites (Babylon)
civs.blurb: Amorite dynasties ruled Babylon, where Hammurabi issued his famous law code. Babylonian math, astronomy and law were inherited by Assyria, Persia and the Greeks.

civs.name: Iranians (Elam, Medes, Persia)
civs.blurb: Elam, then the Medes and Persians, ruled the Iranian plateau. Persia's Achaemenid Empire, with its roads, provinces and religious tolerance, became a model for later empires.

civs.name: India
civs.blurb: From the Indus cities to the Mauryas, Mughals and today's republic, India gave the world decimal numerals with zero, Buddhism and cotton cloth, and is now the most populous nation.
civs.source: Histomap (Sparks 1931); 1949-2024 extension by why-2: width = approx. share of world GDP (PPP) x 1699, from Maddison Project (1950, 1973), a Maddison / IMF WEO blend (1999) and IMF WEO (2024) estimates

civs.name: Huns (steppe nomads)
civs.blurb: Horse-riding nomads of the Eurasian steppe, from the Xiongnu to the Huns. Their raids spurred China's walls, and their push west drove the migrations that helped topple Western Rome.

civs.name: China
civs.blurb: One of the oldest continuous civilizations: paper, printing, the compass and gunpowder spread west from China. Reunified and industrialized, it is now the largest economy by purchasing power.
civs.source: Histomap (Sparks 1931); 1949-2024 extension by why-2: width = approx. share of world GDP (PPP) x 1699, from Maddison Project (1950, 1973), a Maddison / IMF WEO blend (1999) and IMF WEO (2024) estimates

civs.name: Greeks
civs.region: Greece, the Aegean and Mediterranean colonies
civs.blurb: Heirs of the Aegean world, Greek city-states pioneered democracy, philosophy, theater and mathematical proof. Alexander spread Greek culture from Egypt to India, and Rome absorbed it.

civs.name: Assyrians
civs.blurb: Assyria built one of the first great military empires, with iron weapons, mass deportations and Nineveh's library. Nineveh's fall in 612 BCE made room for Babylon and then Persia.

civs.name: Phoenicians & Carthage
civs.region: Levant coast (Lebanon), later the western Mediterranean
civs.blurb: Seafaring traders of Tyre and Sidon spread the alphabet that became Greek and Latin letters. Their colony Carthage rivaled Rome until its destruction in 146 BCE.

civs.name: Hebrews (Israel & Judah)
civs.blurb: The kingdoms of Israel and Judah were small, but their scriptures and belief in one God shaped Judaism, then Christianity and Islam - faiths of over half of humanity today.

civs.name: Kush (Nubia)
civs.blurb: The Kingdom of Kush, called Ethiopia by the Greeks, absorbed Egyptian culture and ruled Egypt itself as its 25th dynasty (c. 744-656 BCE) until Assyria drove it south.

civs.name: Syrians (Aramaeans)
civs.blurb: Aramaean and Neo-Hittite kingdoms rose in Syria after the Hittite collapse. Assyria conquered them, but their Aramaic became the common tongue of the Near East for 1,000 years.

civs.name: Romans / Byzantium
civs.region: Italy and the Mediterranean; later Constantinople
civs.blurb: Rome grew from a city-state into an empire uniting the Mediterranean with roads, law and Latin. Its eastern half, Byzantium, kept Greek learning alive until Constantinople fell in 1453.

civs.name: Lydians
civs.blurb: Lydia in western Anatolia struck the first known coins, from electrum, around 600 BCE. Coined money spread to the Greeks and to the Persians, who conquered Lydia in 546 BCE.

civs.name: Teutons (Germanic peoples)
civs.blurb: Germanic peoples of northern Europe migrated into the weakening Roman world. Goths, Franks, Saxons and others founded the kingdoms from which much of modern Europe grew.

civs.name: Ptolemaic Egypt
civs.blurb: After Alexander, his general Ptolemy made Egypt a Greek-ruled kingdom. Alexandria's Library and Museum made it the ancient world's center of learning, a role it kept under Rome after 30 BCE.

civs.name: Seleucid Empire
civs.blurb: The largest successor state of Alexander's empire, stretching from Syria to Afghanistan. It planted Greek cities across Asia but lost the east to Parthia and the west to Rome.

civs.name: Greco-Bactria
civs.blurb: Greek settlers in Bactria broke away from the Seleucids and pushed into India. Their blend of Greek and Indian art later shaped Gandharan Buddhist sculpture.

civs.name: Parthians
civs.blurb: Iranian horsemen who took Persia from the Seleucids and held off Rome for centuries. As Silk Road middlemen, they profited from the trade between Rome and Han China.

civs.name: Sasanian Persia
civs.blurb: The Sasanians revived Persian power and fought Rome and Byzantium for 400 years. Their mutual exhaustion let Arab armies take Persia and Byzantium's eastern provinces in the 630s-650s.

civs.name: Franks
civs.blurb: A Germanic people who took over Roman Gaul. Under Charlemagne they united much of western Europe, and the division of his empire in 843 created the cores of France and Germany.

civs.name: Western Roman Empire
civs.blurb: The western half of the divided Roman Empire, overrun by Germanic kingdoms by 476. Its fall left the Church and new kingdoms to rebuild western Europe.

civs.name: Arabs (Caliphates)
civs.region: Arabia, then the Middle East, North Africa and Spain
civs.blurb: United by Islam in the 600s, Arab caliphates conquered from Spain to India. Baghdad's scholars preserved Greek science and spread Indian numerals, feeding Europe's later revival.

civs.name: Denmark
civs.blurb: Danish Vikings raided and settled across the North Sea, and Cnut ruled England, Denmark and Norway. Later a small kingdom, Denmark now ranks near the top in wealth and well-being.
civs.source: Histomap (Sparks 1931); 1949-2024 extension by why-2: width = approx. share of world GDP (PPP) x 1699, from Maddison Project (1950, 1973), a Maddison / IMF WEO blend (1999) and IMF WEO (2024) estimates

civs.name: Norway
civs.blurb: Norse seafarers from Norway settled Iceland and Greenland and reached North America around 1000. Norway later joined the Kalmar Union (1397) and stayed under the Danish crown until 1814.

civs.name: Lombards
civs.blurb: A Germanic people who took much of Italy in 568, splitting it from Byzantium. Frankish wars against them (754-774) handed land to the popes, creating the Papal States.

civs.name: Bulgaria
civs.blurb: Turkic Bulgars merged with Slavs to found a Balkan empire that rivaled Byzantium. Its Christian literature in the new Cyrillic script later spread to the Serbs and to Russia.

civs.name: Papacy
civs.blurb: The bishops of Rome inherited Roman prestige and, with Frankish help, ruled central Italy. Popes crowned emperors and launched the Crusades, shaping medieval Europe's politics.

civs.name: Holy Roman Empire / Germany
civs.blurb: The eastern part of Charlemagne's empire grew into a loose empire of German states that lasted until 1806. Prussia unified Germany in 1871, an industrial power at the center of two world wars.
civs.source: Histomap (Sparks 1931); 1949-2024 extension by why-2: width = approx. share of world GDP (PPP) x 1699, from Maddison Project (1950, 1973), a Maddison / IMF WEO blend (1999) and IMF WEO (2024) estimates; continues as Germany (1949-1974 widths count West and East Germany together)

civs.name: France
civs.blurb: West Francia grew into France, long western Europe's most populous state. Its 1789 Revolution spread ideas of rights and nationhood, and Napoleon's wars redrew the map of Europe.
civs.source: Histomap (Sparks 1931); 1949-2024 extension by why-2: width = approx. share of world GDP (PPP) x 1699, from Maddison Project (1950, 1973), a Maddison / IMF WEO blend (1999) and IMF WEO (2024) estimates

civs.name: Normandy (Normans)
civs.region: Northern France, later England and southern Italy
civs.blurb: Vikings granted land by the Frankish king in 911 became the Normans, who conquered England in 1066 and southern Italy, tying Scandinavia, France and England together.

civs.name: Spain
civs.blurb: Christian kingdoms retook Iberia from Muslim rule by 1492, the year Columbus sailed. Spain's empire linked the Americas to Europe and Asia, reshaping world trade, crops and peoples.
civs.source: Histomap (Sparks 1931); 1949-2024 extension by why-2: width = approx. share of world GDP (PPP) x 1699, from Maddison Project (1950, 1973), a Maddison / IMF WEO blend (1999) and IMF WEO (2024) estimates

civs.name: United States
civs.blurb: Born from Britain's American colonies in 1776, the US grew through land, immigration and industry into the largest economy of the 20th century and a leader in science and technology.
civs.source: Not in the Histomap digitization; why-2 estimate placed in free space of each 50-year slice. Width = approx. share of world power (Maddison Project GDP shares as a guide; subjective before 1820); 1949-2024 = approx. share of world GDP (PPP), Maddison Project / IMF WEO. Drawn from the 1774 slice (the thirteen colonies on the eve of independence)

civs.name: Britain
civs.region: Great Britain (England, later the United Kingdom)
civs.blurb: Anglo-Saxon England, remade by the Norman conquest of 1066, developed Parliament and then the Industrial Revolution. Its empire and language carried both around the globe.
civs.source: Not in the Histomap digitization; why-2 estimate placed in free space of each 50-year slice. Width = approx. share of world power (Maddison Project GDP shares as a guide; subjective before 1820); 1949-2024 = approx. share of world GDP (PPP), Maddison Project / IMF WEO. England until 1707, then Great Britain / the United Kingdom; drawn from 1074, just after the Norman conquest

civs.name: Russia
civs.blurb: Muscovy threw off Mongol overlordship in 1480 and expanded across Eurasia to the Pacific. As the USSR it industrialized fast, helped defeat Nazi Germany and rivaled the US for decades.
civs.source: Not in the Histomap digitization; why-2 estimate placed in free space of each 50-year slice. Width = approx. share of world power (Maddison Project GDP shares as a guide; subjective before 1820); 1949-2024 = approx. share of world GDP (PPP), Maddison Project / IMF WEO. Drawn from 1474 (Muscovy under Ivan III); 1949 and 1974 widths are the whole USSR

civs.name: Japan
civs.blurb: Around 600 Japan's court drew on Chinese writing, Buddhism and law to build a state. After 1868 it industrialized at record speed, built an empire, and rebuilt after 1945 into an economic giant.
civs.source: Not in the Histomap digitization; why-2 estimate placed in free space of each 50-year slice. Width = approx. share of world power (Maddison Project GDP shares as a guide; subjective before 1820); 1949-2024 = approx. share of world GDP (PPP), Maddison Project / IMF WEO. Japan's state dates from c. 600, but before 1724 the digitized Chinese band fills the map's eastern edge, so the stream is drawn from 1724

civs.name: Ottoman Empire
civs.region: Anatolia, the Balkans, the Middle East and North Africa
civs.blurb: A Turkish state that rose as Mongol power fractured Anatolia, took Constantinople in 1453 and ruled three continents. Its breakup after World War I created modern Turkey and many Arab states.
civs.source: Not in the Histomap digitization; why-2 estimate placed in free space of each 50-year slice. Width = approx. share of world power (subjective; Maddison Project GDP shares as a guide). Drawn 1324-1874: the empire lasted until 1922, but the next slice (1924) falls after its end

civs.name: Mongols
civs.region: Mongolian steppe, then China, Persia and Russia
civs.blurb: Genghis Khan united the steppe tribes in 1206 and his heirs built the largest contiguous land empire in history. Linking Eurasia, it spread trade, ideas and the Black Death.
civs.source: Not in the Histomap digitization; why-2 estimate placed in free space of each 50-year slice. Width = approx. share of world power (subjective). Drawn 1224-1324 (50-year slices); the unified empire split into khanates after 1260 and the Yuan fell in 1368
